                RADIO TELETYPE TERMINAL EQUIPMENT AN/FGCl OR AN/FGC-1X  “Ty 11l-356

                   SECTION I
                  DESCRIPTION

1. INTRODUCTION.

            a. The Radio Teletype Terminal Equipment AN/FGC1 or AN/FGC-1X forms
   part of a radio-telegraph system, the receiving circuit being designed to
   receive signals alternately from one or two radio transmitters at moderate
   distances. The radio frequencies employed are inthe range of 2 to 26 mnega-
   cycles. A block diagram of the system is shown in figure 3. AN/FGCl equip-
‘ment operates from 50- to 60-cyclae-c power sup anp d Al N/Fy GC-1X from 25- to
  60-cycle supply. The operating and testing procedures are the same for both
   types. Any reference in this book to AN/FGGl equipment applies equally to
  AN/FGC-1X, unless it is stated that the AN/FGC-1X equipment differs.

b. The radio transmitter sends out its normal frequency when the con-

tacts of the telegraph-sending mechanism are closed (marking condition)a,nd

when the contacts are opened (spacing conditio thne )ra,dio frequency is re-

duced 850 cycles, the amplitude remaining unchanged.  At the receiving end

these signals are received in superheterodyne receivers, which invert then

and finally convert them into frequencies in the voice range of about 2125

and 2975 cycles for the closed and open conditions of the sending contacts,

respectively. These voice-frequency signals are rectified in the AN/FGCl

equipment and are passed to the receiving telegraph equipment as d-c tele-

graph signals.

c. Signals are sent by telegraph printer keyboard or automatically by

transmitter-distributor at sixty words per minute.    They are received by

printer or by typing reperforator.

         d. The effect of radio fading is minimized by employing          space diver-
Sity; the receiving equipment is associated with two receiving          antennas which
are spaced several wavelengths apart, and thus the reliability
is greatly increased.                                                    of reception

          e. The circuit is arranged so that when the same radio-frequency as-
Signment is being used for transmitting and receiving, the receiving equip-
ment is disabled while the transmitter isin use. When different frequencies
are used for transmitting and receiving, however, the circuit may be con-
nected so that these two operations can be carried on simultaneousinlyth;is
case, extra printer equipment will ordinarily have to be providefdor sending.
When messages are not being received, each receiver may be connected to both

RADIO TELETYPE TERMINAL EQUIPMENT AN/FGC1 OR AN/#GC-1X  us ae

its pairs of associated antennas in parallsoetlhat signals can be detected
from either distant transmitter. A monitoring circuitis providedto prevent
operation of teletypewriters by noise during this monitoring period. It is
automatically switched out of the circuit when the distant transmitter is
energized.

        f. For an AN/FGCl equipment, 50- to 60-cycle, 103- to 127-volt, or 207-

to 253-volt a-c power supply is required. AN/FGC-1X equip usems e a-cnpt ower
of 25 to 60 cycles, 103 to 127 or 207 to 253 volts. The power may be ob-
tained from commercial sources or other equivalent available supply. To pro-
tect the equipment from humidity, a heater is provided in each cabinet which
is automatically connected to the power supply when the power is switched
off from the radio-receiver and voice-frequency terminal equipment.

         ge The receiving printer equipment can be connected to the AN/FGCl bay
by means of a metallic pair or by a single wire with ground return from the
printer subset. The allowable length of this loop circuit varies greatly,
depending on the type of line facility employed. Its resistance should not
exceed 3700 ohms, as this value would result in the minimum allowable loop
current of 10 milliamperes. In ground-return operation over a composited
pair, the workable distance will usually be determined by crossfire to and
from the telegraph or signal circuit on the other wirofethe pair, and this
will depend on. the type of circuit used on the other wire. Areasonable dis-
tance would be 15 miles of cable or 100 miles of open wire. An ungrounded
rectifier (KS-5844) must be added to an AN/FGCl bay which does not contain
one, when a ground-return loop is used. A filter, not covered in these in-
structions is required in addition to the usual type of composite set to
reduce interference from the telegraph to the telephone circuit.

         h. A location free from abnormal vibration and protected from outside
weather conditions is necessary.

     2 EQUIPMENT.

         a. A bay of AN/FGCl equipment consists of the apparatus for two chan-
nels of a circuit mounted in a metal cabinet 7 feet high, lfoot 10-1/4 inches
wide, and 1 foot 5 inches deep with doors at front and rear, each 1 foot
7-5/8 inches wide. The total weight is about 425 pounds, not crated. When
crated for shipment the weight is about 635 pounds and the over-all dimen-
sions are 7 feet 4 inches x 2 feet 4 inches x 1 foot 9 inches,equivalent to
29.9 cubic feet.

         b. Figures 1 and 2 show the front and rear views of the cabinet with
the doors open. Both doors are hinged at the right as the observer faces
the front, whereas both doors of the radio-receiver cabinet are hinged at
the left. The individual panels on which the equipment is mounted are 19 inches

3. POWER SUPPLY.

         a. The telegraph terminals are completely a-c operated and are equipped
with either of two types of regulated tube rectifiers to supply loop current
and plate voltage to the tubes. The first operates from a power supply of
90 to 60 cycles, 103 to 127 volts or 207 to 253 volts, and the second fron
a supply of 25 to 60 cycles, with the same voltage ranges. A bay may be
adapted for use with either of these two voltage ranges by a screwdriver
change in the internal connections. The rectifier provides a-c filament and
plate voltages. An additional rectifier (disc-type) supplies power to the
receiving loop circuit, when the latter employs ground for the return path
of the current. It operates from a power supply of 25 to 60 cycles, with
the same voltage ranges as the first rectifier. It is connected for 115- or
2380-volt power supply, depending on the position of a lever which is acces-
sible through a small hinged door. The output supplies are permanently ca-
bled to the various panels on the bay.

        b. Two convenience outlets are provided in the front of  the equipment
and two in the rear for appliances which hatv heesame voltage    rating as the
power supply.

          c. For typical power consumption conditions, a carrier-telegraph bay
requires about 140 watts or 160 volt-amperes of a-c power.

4, FREQUENCY CONTROL.

         Most bays of AN/FGCl equipment contain a circuit for controlling auto-
matically the frequency of the received audio signals. Since the connection
to the receiver bay for frequency control is high impedancet,he control pair
Should have high insulation resistance.

    5. FREQUENCY SHIFT.

The terminal equipment is designed and these instructions have been

written for use with a radio circuit in which there is a frequency change

of 850 cycles, normally, between marking and spacing signals. The following

table shows recommended values of this frequency shift for various frequency

bands, but these recommendations are only tentative and so are subject to

change. These instructions do not describe the circuit arrangements or the

changes in operating procedures involved, when the frequency shift is other

than 850 cycles.                     |

                  Frequency Band           Carrier Shift

                     70 = 500 ke           170 cycles
                   900 - 2000 ke           340 cycles
                  above 2000 ke            850 cycles

6. CHANGES IN EQUIPHENT.

        a. Some bays of earlier manufacture have left the factory with the
disc-type rectifier omitted but without the necessary wiring arrangements
to permit the use of the regulated tube rectifier for supply of loop cur-
rent. Instructions for making these wiring changes are given in paragraph 8h,

       be.  Most  bays are equipped  at the factory with temporary wiring in ac-
cordance    with  paragraph 8h, for  the regulated tube rectifierto furnish loop
current.

         c. Twenty regulated tube rectifiers were wired according to the color
codes which are crossed out on the wiring diagram, figure 46 (see note l15o0f

fig. 46). The AN/FGC] bays containing them have twenty of the following

twenty-four serial numbers: 2, 3, 4, 7, 10-13, 17, 18, 20-25, 27, 28, 31,
33, 38, 39, 40, and 45. In all other bays, the color codes are normal,

         d. Many bays were equipped with monitoring circuits which required a
steady closure of the control relay in the radio-receivebary. Instructions
are given in paragraph 8j to modify the wiring sothat they will work with only a
nonentary closure. Baysof later manufacture, will be furnished with this wiring.

8. INSTALLATION AND INITIAL PROCEDURE.

a. Remove the AN/FGCl cabinet from its crate and, unless another loca-

tion is specified, place it beside the radio-receiver cabinet to the right

as you face the fronts of the two cabinets.    Allow -at least a 2-1/2-foot

clearance in front to the nearest wall or other obstruction, 2-1/2 feet at

the back, and a 2-foot clearance around one enofdthe two cabinets for pas-

sageway. A clearance of 3 to 4 feet-is desirable, both front and rear. The

cabinet should be situated in a place reasonably free from vibration on a

firm footing, preferably concrete. It should be fastenteo dthe floor, uti-

_lizing holes in the bottom corner brackets of the cabinet and lag or expansion

screws, and it should be bolted to the receiver bay. Install copper-bonding

braids between the two cabinets at top and bottom, scraping off the paint

under the braids where they are bolted to the cabinets in order that there

may be a good electrical contact.

         b. Make the following external connections to the AN/FGCl bay (refer
to the application schematic fig. 36). External connections are brought into
the cabinet through cable holes at the top or bottom. Any wires involved
which pass from top to bottom inside of the cabinet shobue l tiedd to cabinet
channel brackets. The bay terminal strip is at the topof the bay. In order
to make the shielded pairs short from the limiters to the radio outputs on
the adjacent bay (see paragraphs (2) and (8) belruo n tw hem)th, rough a bot-
tom hole at the left into a facing hole in the radio-receiver bay, unless
local conditions dictate otherwise.

              (1) Connect an 8-guage wire from waterpipe or other good ground to
the ground punching on the cabinet upright (lower left as you face the back).

             (2) Shielded pair from terminals 1A and  2A (termina1lasnd 2of   ter-
minal strip A) of the channel A current limiter       tothe A radio-receiver  ter-
minals OUTPUT 6002 and GND. Connect the shield        to terminal 2A.

            (3) Shielded pair from  terminals   1A and 2A of channel B_ current

limiter to the B radio-receiver     terminals  OUTPUT 600° and GND. Connect the
shield to terminal 2A.

ll. OVER-ALL CURRENT.

         a.  Figure 6  is a schematic drawionf gone terminoaf lthe             over-all cir-
cuit. A      complete  circuit includes another similar terminal               at a distant
place.

            b. In the radio transnitter circuit, signals fron the telegraph-sending
- Gircuit control the frequency of the radio signals. During mar thektrs ans-

  nitter puts out its normal frequency as determined by the transmitter ex-
  citer. During spaces the frequency of the radio signalis reduced 850 cycles.
  Different radio frequencies are used in the band from 2.4 to 26 megacycles
  and any one transmitter may use one of several frequencies in this range,
  the particular frequency chosen depending upon the length of path, the time
  of day, and the season.

Caerebethemrecciving stavion, radio Signals are received ins two dit-

ferent antennas spaced several wavelengths apart. Radio waves at the fre-

quencies used in this system are subject to fading. The signal arrives at

either antenna over two or more changing paths of different lengths and the

waves over these paths may neutralize or reinforce each other depending upon

their respective phase relations.  When the phase relationasre such that

they neutralize in one antenna, however, the phase relations are different

in the other antenna spaced a few wavelengths away and so will not usually

neutralize each other in the second antenna. Thus by using two antennas in

a space-diversity receiving arrangement, there will usually be’a good signal

in one or the other.

d. Each antenna is connected to a. superheterodyne radio receiver in

which the signals are demodulated. The marking signal becomes 2125 cycles

at the output of the radio receiver and the spacing signal, 2975 cycles.

These frequency values are nominal, and the receiving equipment is designed

to tolerate a total variatiofo+n800 cycles for the transmitted frequencies

and the beat frequencies of the receivers combined. The two channeoflsthe

receiving diversity circuit are designated channel Aand channelB. The sig-

nals in channel A pass from the radio receiver through a 7-db pad and an

input filter to a LIMITER.  The filter passes all frequencies within both

the marking and spacing bands but excludes noise frequencies outside of

these bands. In the limiter, the signals are amplified andthe action of the

limiter is such that it delivers a substantially constant output for wide

         e. Two sets of antennas may be provided to communicate with two dif-
ferent distant points; in this case, a control circuit enables the operator
at the telegraph station to connect the radio transmitter and receivers to
either or both sets of these. This latter connection is used, normally, only
to monitor circuits in which the distant transmitters are not energized. A
monitoring circuit, in this case, keeps the teletype equipment from respond-
ing to noise and is automatically restored to normal when a steady marking
signal is received longer than about 1/4 second.

 Simultaneously.

or spacing signal and are expressedin db below a milliwatt. Levels at the

fade. Preceding the limiter, however,the levels fluctuate widely from about
10 db greater than their nominal values to many db less.

13. RADIO RECEIVER.

           Each radio receiver is of the superheterodyne type, employing oscil-
 lators which are common to the two receivers. Inthe first stage, the output
 of a high-frequency oscillator modulates the incoming signal, reducingit to
 a frequency of about 465 kilocycles. This internediate frequency is again
 modulated by means of a second oscillator, which is adjusted so that beat
‘frequencies of about 2125 and 2975 cycles result in the audio output for
 marking and spacing frequencies respectively. This second oscillatmaoy rbe
 either crystal or manually controlled. In receiving terminals equipped with
 automatic-frequency control, either the automatic-frequency or crystal con-
 trol may be employed. The automatic-frequency control should usually keep
the audio frequencies within +50 cycles of their nominal values. When this
 control is not used, the frequencies should not be allowed to depart more
than +300 cycles from their nominal values.

         a. The INPUT FILTER passes a frequency band of about 1600 to 8600 cy-
cles. A typical loss characteristic plotted against frequency is given in
figure 7. The pass band of this filtie s mrade wide enough to pass both the
marking and spacing signals when the frequencies of these signals vary over
the range of +800 cycles.

         b. The M CH FILTER  passes a band of about 1700to 2500 cycles.   A typ-
ical loss characteristic     of this and of the spacing filter is shown  in fig-
ea ae

c. The S CH FILTER passes a band of about 2600 to 3400 cycles.

of the  (1) The purpose of the monitoring circuitis to prevent the operation
nected  receiving printer equipment by noise when the radio receivers are con-

   not energized or when the receiving circuit is disabled because the local

   its normal receiving condition and the monitoring circuit itselfis restored
   to its nonnonitoring condition. If two radio circuits have been monitored
   Simultaneously, the receivers must be disconnected fromthe idle circuit be-

   relay contacts are closed for more than 0.1 second during the switching op-

               (2) Figure 15 shows a monitoring circuit in schematic form. When

   the relay contacts in the radio-receiver cabinet are closed, they connect
   the negative terminal of the telegraph rectifier -TB to the winding of re-
   lay A, operating it. Relay B is normally operated. The top upper contacts
¢ (fourth and third) of relay A ground the spacing winding of the receiving
   relay through 6905 ohms, thus tending to hold it on the spacing contact.
   Noise may cause it to leave this contact momentarily but this will have no
  effect as long as it does not touch the marking contact for more than about
   1/4 second. The first and second top contacts of relay A operate relay C.
   The bottom contacts of A connect -TB through 1400 ohms to the loop, thus
   holding the loop relay in the subset steadily on its marking contact and so
   preventing the operation of the printer equipment due to noise. The opera-
   tion of the left hand contacts of relay C disconnect the winding of relay B
   from the positive terminal of the telegraph rectifier +TB, whihacs h held it
   operated, and connect it to the armature of the REC relay. As noted above,
   this armature is held on the spacing contact which also is connected to +TB
   and so relay B, which is slow releasing, remains operated. The right-hand
   contacts of relay C connect -TB to the winding of relay A, through contacts
   of B, holding A operated.

   the frequency which corresponds to a marking signal, the REC relay operates
   to its marking contact, causing relay B to release. The release of relay B
   releases relay A which in turn releases relay C. Relay Bthereupon operates
   again.

                 (4) Connections from the telegraph rectifier to either REC relay
   circuit pass through contacts of the REC REL IN CKT 2 jacks. When no plugs
   are in these jacks, the circuit of REL 1 is energized; when plugs are in,

     20. FREQUENCY-CONTROL CIRCUIT.

         a. A view of the frequency-control panelis shown in figure 18 and the
circuit in figure 17. This circuit is designed to. keep the marking audio
frequency delivered to the AN/FGC1l equipment by the radio receivers within
+50 cycles of 2125 cycles. If the frequency deviates from 2125 cycles, a
d-c voltage appears in the output of this circuit which causes a compensating
change in the frequency of the radio-receiver output. The marking frequency
passes through the IN filter to the control grid of tube V2 which amplifies
it and it is further amplified in tube V3. The output of V3 contains two branches,
In one branch a portion of the output passes through a Q.l-microfarad ca-
pacitor and a potentiometer which impresses one-half of the output voltage
on the plates of double diode V4. The cathode of V4 is biased about +23 volts

                                                                43


---

TM 11-356          SIGNAL CORPS
     29

by means of the 130-volt supply acting through a potentiometer. Ifthe peak

voltage of the a-c output of tube V3 exceeds about46 volts, therefore, pulses

of current will pats o gs round through V4, increasing the charge of the 0.1-
microfarad capacitor. As in other similar AVC circuits, the resulting cur-
rent through the resistor-capacitor network which is connected between the
plates of V4 and ground impresses a negative potentioan lthe gri of dtube V2.
This ig a variable gain tube, and so its gain is reduced. Thus tube V4 and
its associated circuit acts asan automatic volume control and maintains the
output of V3 substantially constant with a peak voltage somewhat greater
than 46 volts. A negative potentialis impressed on the control gri of d tube
Vl by the AVC circuit, which is twice the value impressed on V2. When V3
has its above normal output, this potential is sufficient to disable vl.

          b. If the radio receivers are so far ouofttune that the received fre-
quency will not pass through the IN filter, i.e., if it is outside the linits
of about 1600-2600 cycles, tube Vl will be active. This tube acts as a by-
pass of the IN filter andthe circuit constants are such that the loss through

this by-pass is greater than the loss in the pass band of the filter. The

automatic-frequency control, responding to this frequency, will bring the

received frequency within the pass band of the filter and Vl will then be

disabled, as explained above.

c. The second output of V3 is impressed on a high-pass and a low-pass

filter in parallel, which act asa discriminator. These filters are adjusted

to have the same losses at 2125 cycles by the FREQ ADJ knob. The outputs

of the two filters are rectified in V5, which is a double diode connected

to form two half-wave rectifiers. When the frequency is 2125 cycles, equal

currents pass through the two diodes and so no voltage exists across the

output terminals.  If the frequency is lower than 2125 cycles, it passes

freely through the upper filter to the upper diode whereas the lower filter

allows little or no current in the lower diode. Thus the upper output ter-

minal has a positive potential with respectto the lower terminal. Similarly,

if the frequency is higher than 2125 cycles, the lower terminal is positive

with respect to the upper. Since the latter is grounded, the upper in this

case will be negative with respect to ground.

        d. The output delivered to the controlled oscillator is +1 volt for a
frequency departure of about +60 cycles from 2125 cycles. This control volt-
age acts upon the tuning of the intermediate frequency oscillator of the
radio receivers to keep the marking frequency approximately 2125 cycles and
it is expected that the maximum deviation from this value will be approxi-
mately 50 cycles. If one volt in the control pair causes a change in fre-
quency of 1000 cycles in the radio receiversa,nd if the uncontrolled frequency
is 2125 + 1060 cycles the control voltage tendsto increase toa value much “a
greater than-l volt. But as it increasest,he intermediate oscillator changes

 cycles, establishing equilibrium, and so the controlled frequency will re-

-eycle correction). The circuit controls the marking frequency in the range
 2000 cycles below to several thousand cycles above 2125 cycles. The maxinun

          e. The automatic-frequency-control circuit will tune the receiver in
l or 2 seconds if the transmitter is energized after being “off the air" for
over 10 seconds. If under operating conditions, however, the frequency snould
suddenly be changed several hundred cycles, it would take about 10 seconds
for the receiver to be retuned, because the delay circuit associated with
the control grid of tube Vl must discharge before this tube can become ac-

lished. <A steady spacing signal lasting over 5 seconds, therefore, should
be avoided.

f. Tube Operation.

              (1) Fhe tubes are of the 3-element, gas-filled type and the point
in the a-c cycle at which they start firing (conducting current) is con-
trolled by the negative grid bias or difference between the voltage of the
grid and the filament. In general, the greater the negative grid bias the
higher the plate voltage must be before the current starts to flow, but for

                                 49


---

TM 11-356                 SIGNAL CORPS
     rt

any tube there is a critical grid negative bias beyond which the tube will

not fire. After starting to fire, a tube continues to conduct current for
the rest of the a-c half-cycle and the output current, and therefore the

maintained voltage, depends on how much of each half-cycle each tube is fir-

ing. Vl fires during one half-cycle and V2 during the other, which gives

full-wave rectification.      Changes  in output voltage are  reflected through
the grid-control circuit  to change    the output and return  the voltage to the

regulated value.

              (2) At light loads it is not necessary for the tubes to fire every
cycle as the electrolytic capacitors carry the load for a few cycles during
which time the grid bias is enough to prevent firing of the tubes. When the

output voltage decreases below the regulated value, the tubes fire again for
a few cycles to recharge the capacitors. This type of operation is evidenced
by a flicker in the glow within the tubes and vibration of the needle of the
voltmeter. At extremely light loads, firing of one tube only is sufficient
to maintain the output voltage at regulated value. Even at heavy load, and
with the tubes loaded approximately equally, the glow from the tubes will
not necessarily be uniform, due to variations in temperature and physical
characteristics of the tubes.

             (3) Cathode trouble usually consists of open filament or low emis-
Sion. With low emission the tube will glow and appear normal but still be
unsatisfactory. Grid trouble may be high firing point or grid emission.
High firing point is the condition where too high plate voltageis necessary
to fire the tube. While this can be compensated to some extent by changes
in the setting of rheostat R, the tube is inclined to be unstable at light
loads and high line voltages. It should be replaced if causing erratic oper-
ation. Grid emission sometimes occurs due to cathode material which has been
carried over to the grid. The effect of this is negligible until thempem.
perature of the tube becomes high enough to cause this active material on
the grid to give off electrons which causes thé ‘grid to lose control, re-=
sulting in high output voltage. This effect disappears as the tube cools so
that satisfactory operation may be possible at light loads when it is not
possible at full load.

23. RECEIVING RELAY.

      a. The receiving relay, sho inwfin gure 23, is polar-tyip.ee.,,it oper-

ates to one contact for one polarofict urryent through a winding and to the

other contact for current in the other direction. The windings surround a

permalloy armature, to one endof which contacts are fastened. The armature

projects between two pole pieces, one of which is made a north pole, and the

other a south pole by means of a permanent magnet. A rough explanation of

the operation of the relay is as follows: Current through a winding in one

direction magnetizes the armature, causing the end which passes between the

pole pieces to become a north pole and the other end a south. The north pole

is attracted toward the south pole piece. Current inthe opposite direction

magnetizes the armature in the opposite direction, causing it to be attracted

toward the north pole piece.     In the telegraph terminal, marking current

flows through one winding to cause the relay to operate to the marking

contact, whereas spacing current flows through an equal and opposite wind-

ing to operate the relay to its spacing contact.

         b. If the permanent magnet is removed fromthe relay and replaced, its
magnetic,strength is weakened. Though the relay can usually be given an
operating adjustment after that, the gaps between the armature and pole pieces
will have to be made considerably smaller and more trouble will be experi-
enced from magnetic particles inthe gaps. Therefore do not remove the mag-

24. FREQUENCY-INDICATOR CIRCUIT.

         a. <A front view of the frequency-indicator panelis shown in figure 24,
and a schematic drawing infigure 25. Inthis circuitt,he markani d n spag cing
carrier frequencies from an output branch of the limiter in channel A are
modulated by a frequency of 2550 cycles. These are normally 2125 and 2975
cycles, respectively, and the difference product, normally 425 cycles, is
separated from other products by a filter and passed through an inductance,
the voltage drop across which is proportional to the frequency. This volt-
age is amplified and rectified, resulting in a direct current which is pro-
portional to the frequency, andthe indication of a d-c meter in the path of
this current is a measure of the frequency. If the marking and spacing fre-
quencies are normal, the center-zero meter will indicate zero. If they are
symmetrically located about 2550 cycles and donot differ by 850 cycles, the
meter deflection will be steady but will be negative (to the left of zero)
if the frequency separation is less than 850 cycles, positive if greater.
If the frequencies are not symmetrically locatedt,he meter indications will
be unsteady. The radio receiver is tunedto matk he e meter indication steady;
if it then indicates more than +15, the transmitter station should be noti-
fied that the frequency separation is wrong. The frequencies of channel B
can be measured by patching its CURR LIM B jack to the FREQ IND IN jack,
but this is not necessary, since the oscillators are common to the two re-
ceivers and ensure that the audio frequencies will be identical.

         b. Oscillator.—Referring to figure 25, the cathode of tube VA is con-
nected to terminal 2 of the winding of an autotransformer OSC, and the full
winding 1-3 is connected from the griofdthe tutb o gre ound. An alternating
voltage existing in the cathode circuit, therefore, will cause an emf be-
tween terminals 1 and 3 of the transformer. Since this is impressed upon
the control grid of the tube, this circuit forms an oscillator. The fre-
quency is adjusted to be 2550 cycles at the factory by a capacitance of ap-
proximately 0.15 microfarad connected to the coil terminals.

            c. Modulator.—The marking and spacing curreonf tabsout 2125 and 2975
  cycles respectively pass from the CURR LIM A jack through a filter which
  attenuates frequencies above about 4000 cycles and a ZERO ADJ potentiometer
 to grid 8 of the tube VA. The modulation resulting from the interaction of
these frequencies with the 2500-cycle oscillator frequency produces in the
  output:

                                                    2050-2125 = 425 cycles

                                                     2975-2500 = 425 cycles

 A filter consisting of two coils with associated capacitors passes any fre-
  quency below about 1000 cycles and attenuates higher frequencies.

d. Discriminator.—From the output of the filter mentioned above, the

425-cycle current is connected to coil D through 30,000 ohms. The 80,000-

ohm impedance is large compared to that of the 3.1 henrys in coil D and so

the current will be substantially independent of frequency. Coil D acts as

a discriminator, since the voltage drop across it will be directly propor-

tional to the frequency; this proportionality is made more -constant by a

small bridged capacitance. It will be recalled that the out ofp theulit miter

is constant except during deep fades and is independent of frequency; the

output of the oscillator too is substantially constant; andso the resulting

modulation product will be substantially constant in amplitude. Therefore,

the voltage drop across the discriminator is directly proportional to fre-

quency and may be used to measure it.       This voltage is applied to the con-

trol grid of tube VB.

         e. Calibration.—When the CAL button is depressed, the gridof tube VB
is connected toa potentiometer which is in parallel with the discriminator;
the voltage then does not vary with frequency. This potentiometer is ad-
justed at the factory so that the voltage applied to the grid is the same
as that across the discriminatcooril for 425 cycles, andso causes the fre-
quency indicator meter to indicate zero. The process of calibration, then,
consists in depresstihne gCAL button and adjusttihenZgERO ADJ potentiometer
until the meter indicates zero.

         f. Meter Circuit.—The 425-cycle current in the output of amplifier
tube VB is rectified in a half-wave copper-oxide rectifier and the resulting

                               SECTION IV
                               MAINTENANCE

   £0. GENERAL.

|  Service failures will be kept to a minimum by careful handling of the

equipment during installation and operation and by exercising cair n me aking

field repairs and adjustments on the apparatus.  Do not disturb the wiring

any more than is' necessary in testing or inspecting for troubles and, if a

soldering iron is used, take care to prevent dropping splashes of solder on

apparatus parts or wiring terminals.      Keep the parts as free from dirt as

possible by keeping the can covers on apparatus except when it is necessary

to remove them for maintenance purposes. Also, do not keep open the doors

of the cabinet unnecessarily.

   26. TROUBLE ANALYSIS.

          a. When trouble develops, and from a preliminary    analysis    of the con-
dition, it appears that a particular iten of equipment      may be at      fault, make
the tests in paragraph 9 for that item in an attempt        to find      the cause of
trouble.

         b. In determining what iten of equipmentis at fault,it will be helpful
to keep in mind the symmetry of this telegraph system. It contains two -re-
ceiving channels which have identical electric circuits. Furthermore, each
of these channels has marking and spacing branches which are similar ex-
cept that they pass different frequencies. A convenient method for deter-
Mining what item of equipment is causing the trouble is to "frog" the two
channels at the various jacks, in turn, where this is practicable. For ex-
ample, if theisrre eason to suspect that the trouble isin a detector, patch
it into the good channel and pat the c deth ector from the latter into the bad
channel. If the trouble changes to the other channel, it is an indication
that the suspected detector is in trouble.

          c. A suggested procedure in locating trouble follows. It need not be
adhered to rigidly if experience or some clue as tothe locatiofonthe trou-
ble suggests a short cut. Before following this procedure, test the receiv-
ing relay or replace it by a spare, and make any simple tests which the nature
of the trouble suggests.

              (1) If practicable, obtain printer signals or reversals, depending
on the nature of the trouble, from the local transmitter and observe them in
a printer, typing reperforator, or on the meter which measures loop current,

                                      O°


---

TM 11-356                        SIGNAL CORPS
     26

respectively. If the trouble is not present, it was probably at the trans-
nitting end or due to unusual radio conditions. There is a possibility how-
ever, that it is in the radio receivers, since they will usually be receiving
local signals at a much higher level than signals from the distant trans-

mitter.

           (2) Patch DET OUT CH A jacks to REC REL IN CKT 1 jacks and repeat

the tests. Repeat with DET OUT CH B jacks patchteodREC REL IN CKT 1 jacks.
This will determine whether the troubleis in channel A or B. If the trouble

has disappeared, it is probably  inthe noise-suppression circuitsor the wir-
ing associatewidth these jacks.  These patches disable the noise-suppression

circuits.  If the trouble is in both channels, it is presumably in the re-

ceiving relay circuit, the loop, or the substation equipment. To see if it

is in the receiving relay circuit, patch in the no. 2 circuit by patching

DET OUT CH A to REC REL IN CKT 2 and REL OUT 2 to REC LOOP jacks. Resor

the results of tests.

              (3) Frog the circuit by patching from PAD OUT of CHANNEL A to CH
FILTS IN of channel B and PAD OUT of channel B to CH FILTS IN of channel A.
Repeat the tests in paragraph (2) and record the results. If the trouble is
in the same channel as it was before, it is behind the frogging point; if
the trouble has changed channels, it is aheoafdthe frogging point. Remove |
all patches.

             (4) If the results obtained in paragraph (3) indicate that the trou-
ble is aheorabed hind the frogging point, frog at other points inturn which
precede or follow, respectively, the PAD OUT jacks in the circuit, and re=
peat the tests in paragraph (2) recording the results, until the trouble is
located. The patches required to frog at various jacks are given in the
table below. Keep in mind that if the trouble changes from one channel to
the other when the channels are frogged,as compared with the channelin which
the trouble was located in paragraph (2), the trouble is ahead of the frog-

ging point.

   27. TROUBLE LOCATION.

   a. When it has been determined that there is trouble in a particular

item of equipment, either by the nature of the trouble indication or by the

procedures in paragraph 26, the next step is to determine the actual cause

of the troubte such as a defective tube, wiring trouble, etc. To do this,

make check tests, such as measuring the voltage from each vacuum tube ter-

minal to ground or as specified otherwise, according to the table in para-

graph 34. Test the vacuum tubes.        Inspect the wiring and make continuity

tests with an ohmmeter.

         b. A Western Electric Co. KS-8295 volt-ohmmeter orits equivalent, for
voltage and resistance measurements, will probably be sufficient for most
trouble location tests. This volt-ohmmeter mabeyused for measuring either
a-c or d-c voltages or resistances and for checking capacitors for short
circuits or grounds any other available volt-ohmmeter having aninternal re-
Sistance of at least 1000-ohms per volt may be used.

   CAUTION: Do not use a buzzer or other insensitive    device for con-
      tinuity tests as it may harm a coil. Safe direct  current through
      any coil winding is the amount passed by 6 volts  in series with
      1000 ohms, connected tothe winding. Do not’ send  direct current
       through the 716C Receiver.

To check the loss ina     pad, measure  each  component resistance and compare
with values in the list   of parts.

          e. If a cathode-ray oscilloscope is available, it will be a useful
testing tool for locating trouble. When similar ite of em quis pment are avail-
able, for instance, tho of s chae nnels A and B, the indications on the oscil-
loscope screen when connection is made to various parts of the good and
defective equipment, in turan nd ,they are energibyzsetedady signals or re-
versals, will usually show whether an item of equipment is in trouble.

          e. Wiring Diagrams.—In locating trouble it may be necessary to refer
to the wiring diagrams. In these diagrams (see List of Jllustrations for
fig. numbers) each pioe f ac ppae ratus has the same designataisotnhat stamped
on the equipment, and the wiring terminals on each piece of apparatus are
shown in their proper relative locationas viewed fromthewiring side. Some
wiring diagrams employ the "airline" system of showing connections. With
this system, each piece of apparatusis arbitrarily numbered and lines, called
feed lines, representing the individual wires are carried a short distance
and terminated at a common or base line running at right angles to the feed
lines. These feed lines are marked with the color of the wire and have a
number near the base line which is the same as’ the number of the piece of
apparatus to whithc e ohther endof the wire connects. If two figure numbers
appear on a feed line, it means that there are two wires one from each of
the indicated figures. If the number "2" precedes the color code, both wires
are of the sane color. It is not necessary to trace a connection through
the common or base line and no provision is made for doing so. By observing
the color and identification number, it is possible to move directly to the
other end of the wire. Inaddition to obvious color abbreviations, the fol-
lowing are used: BL for blue, BK for black, G for green, and S for slate or gray.

28. FUSE ALARMS.

       When a fuse on the fuse-alarm panel blows, the buzzer sounds. The blown

fuse is indicated by its glass bead being out of line with the beads of the

other fuses. When the fuse is removed, the buzzer stops.  In replacing a

fuse, make sure that it is put in place right side up, otherwise the buzzer

will not sound when the fuse blows.      The color of the glass bead indicates

the current rating of the fuse. This ratiin s aglso stamped on one terminal.

The fuses in the rectifiers are not of the alarm type and the buzzer will

not sound when one of these fuses blows.

               (3) Contact Burnishing.—When necessary to clean the contacts, bur-
nish them using a clean no. 266 blade of the no. 265C contact burnisher. It
is very important to keep clean the blades of the contact burnishers and any
thickness gauges which are used on the contacts. These should be wiped off
with a clean dry cloth before being placed against each contact and fre-
quently wiped with a clean cloth dampened with carbon tetrachloride.

              (4) In burnishing normally-open contacts, place the blade of the
burnisher between the contacts, and operate the relay nlanually giving a
slight pressure against the blade of the burnisher, at the same time moving
the blade back and forth. The desired result is usually obtained by rubbing
the burnisher between the contacts two or three times. In the case of nor-
nally-closed contacts, the tension of the springs themselves will usually
furnish sufficient pressure against the burnisher. On springs having heavy
tension, lift one of the springs away to insert the burnisher.

(3) Spring Tension.

                  (a) Spring tensions are specifiedin figure 32 on a mininum basis.
They have, however, in the case of moving springs (springs which do not rest
against the spoolhead) a direct bearing on the electrical performance of the
relay and if they are greatly in excess of the specified mininum, the relay
may fail to meet its electrical requirements, in which case the tension will
have to be reduced. In readjusting,it is desirable to have as much tension
in the moving springs as is consistent with meeting the other requirements.
Attempt to distribute the tension of the moving springs proportionately be-
tween the top and bottom spring conbinations.

            (b) If a spring is excessively bowed or bent or if there is not a

noticeable clearance between springs, straightetnhe spring before adjusting

to meet the spring tension requirement.                To straighten a spring, span it

with the slotted end of the proper spring adjuster just back of the bow or

bend and while exerting      pressure to the right or    left, as   required, draw the
Spring adjuster forward      the length of the bow.         Repeat  this operation as

required until the spring is approximately straight.  Take care when making
this adjustment to avoid tilting the spring.

                 (c) To adjust a spring for tension, span it with the slotted end
of the proper spring adjuster just back of the stud and slide the adjuster
to the base of the spring. Adjust the spring by applying at the handle end
of the tool, slight sidewise pressureto the right or left as required, thus
tending to bend the spring at its base. Exercise care not to disturb adja-
cent springs and avoid twisting the spring.

                (d) If the desired tension canbn e oo btat ined by adjusting as out-

lined in paragraph (c) above, without bowing the spring too much, apply the
proper spring adjuster to the spring just bacofkthe stud and slide it back
to the base of the spring. Then, draw the adjuster forward the length of
the spring, meanwhile applying pressure as required so that the spring is
formed into a slight gradual bow with its concave surface facing the arma-
ture. Then move the adjuster to the base of the spring and adjustas covered
in paragraph (c). The magnitude of the bow to be formed in the spring nust
be learned by experience and should be such that whenthe final tension ad-
justment is made at the base the spring will be approximately straight.

(4) Adjustment For Pressure of Armature Against Adjusting Nut.—If

the armature is not held against the adjusting nut with the pressure speci-

fied in figure 32, increase the tension of the D and A springs which are

tensioned against the armature as outlined in paragraph (3)(c) above.  In

making this adjustment, increase the tensionotfhe spring farthest from the

armature first and if the desired pressure cannot be obtained by adjusting

this spring alone, adjust the other springs which hold the armature against

the adjusting nut as required. Itis not necestosdiastr riy bute the tension

of all A and D springsin any particular combination equally. However, take

care in making the adjustment that the combined pressure of the A and D

springs of the top combination is approximately equal to that of the bottom

combination. To check this, blo thec armk ature unoperated and place the tip

of the 70J gauge against the spring nearest the armature. Read the tension

when a clearance is noticeable between the stud and the armature.

these springs should be so adjusted that there isa slight clearance between

        (8) Examine the armature assembly for loosenofersivsets which hold

the armature spring to the armature proper. If these appear to be loose,

renove the armature and tighten these rivets so that the springs are firmly

held to the armature. The armature contact spring should be approximately

               (4) Replace the armature if it has been removed. With two roundhead
armature mounting screws loosened, and with a .005-inch thickness gauge be-
tween the armature and the left pole face, hold the armature fully operated
by applying pressure to the armature on a line midway between the two pole
faces and tighten the armature mounting screws. Replace terminal screw D.

             (5) Adjust the armature tension spring with long-nose pliers until
the pressure at the end of the spring is 150 +25 grams.

place by means of the long-nose pliers applied at the bend of the spring, so
that the armature is tensioned away from the coils with a pressure of 20 to
00 grams measuredat a point opposite the center of the right pole face.

            (7)  Adjust the armature back stop bracket (opposite right pole face)
until there      is a .010-inch (+.001 inch) clearance between the armature stop
pin and the      right pole face with no current flowing in the coils.

                (8) Adjust the position of the gong and bend the armature extension
  if necessary, until the following requirement is met: With the armature
fully operated and the gong screw tightened, the clapper should just clear
  the gong at a point about 1/16 inch from the open side of the gong.

gong poSition and armature spring tension to obtain         the most satisfactory
sound of the bell.

32. POWER RECTIFIERS.

        a. Regulated Tube Rectifier.

        (1) Timer.—The reset timer in the X-61680B rectifier is arranged

for adjustment of the time of operation but this adjustment should not be

changed. The timer requires no lubrication or contact maintenance.       It

should be replaced if its switch does not operate in normal operation time

‘see par. 8e(4). after connecting the power and restore within 5 seconds after

power is disconnected. Release time is 0.2 to 0.5 second.                Operation and

                                      AL


---

TH 11-356                        SIGNAL CORPS
      39

release are indicated by a slight click in the contact box. Restore time
is the time required for the rotating dise to return to normal after power

is disconnected. The amount of travel of the spring arm after operation of
the switch, and measured at the end of the switch box, should be approxi-
nately 1/8 inch. This travel controls the release time and permits instan-
taneous operation of the rectifier after power failures of suchshort duration

that filaments have not cooled. It need not be checked if the rectifier
seens to be operating satisfactorily. Travel can be adjusted by loosening

the lock nut on the stop screw on the spring arm and turning the screw, as

required. The above also applies to the reset timers used on X-616800 rec-

tifiers except that neither the operation time nor the travel of the spring

arm after operation of the switch are adjustable.

              (2) Varistor Replacement.—Failure of a varistor may be caused by
high voltage or a prolonged overload. Replace if the voltage readings are
less than 8 volts for varistor H, less than 42 volts for varistors A and B,
or less than 4.5 volts for varistor C used in rectifiers C.

              (3) Thermistor and Associated Resistor.—When thermistor T    or re-
sistor C is replaced, select the C resistor tap that agrees with the     resist-
ance value stamped on the thermistor being used.

b. Dise-type Rectifier (KS-5844).

              (1) When the rectifier is connectedto either a 115- or 230-volt a-c
input power supply and there is no d-c output as indicated by the equipment
neter, check for a blown line fuse. Should the fubs e be lown, ascertain the
cause of its failure before inserting a new one. If the input power supply
is 280 volts, check the position. of the toggle lever. If fuse and lever are
satisfactory, check point-to-point voltage readings given in paragraph 33
to locate part of circuit not functioning. Check circuit continuitotlyo-
cate a defective piece of equipment for replacement.

             (2) When making a continuity test, disconnect the input power from
the rectifier, and where parallel paths are present inthe rectifier circuit
it may be necessary to disconnect one of the leads.

             (3) Replacement of  Varistor.—Failure of the varistor may be caused
by a high input voltage or       by a prolonged overload on the rectifier. The

varistor should be replaced       when the d-c output voltage approaches the low
voltage limit with the two       adjusting switches turned to the. extreme right
or high-voltage position.

          c. llectrolytic Capacitors.—Replace electrolytic capacitors in the
power-supply units with new ones about 3-1/2 years after the date onthe ca-
pacitor. If the rectifiers are not in use, operate them temporarily for
1/2 hour every 18 months to restore the film on the electrolytic capacitor

RADIO TELETYPE TERMINAL EQUIPMENT AN/FGCl or AN/FGC-1X  ee

plates. These capacitors are marked Cl ito C8, Cl to Cl0, and Cl and C2,
respectively, in rectifiers X-61680B, X-61680C, and KS-5844. Connect spare
electrolytic capacitors to the positive 130-volt supply for 1/2 hour every
18 months. To do this, disconnect the power from the AN/FGCl equipment (dial
02 and check that the heater lamps light); connect the + terminoaf lthe ca-
pacitor to the output of the regulated tube rectifier (not the KS-5844)
through one of the 35R or 85S fuses. or 74E heat coils, and a mounting lug
(negative terminal) to ground; connect power to the bay (dial 01) and leave
for 1/2 hour; then disconnect the power again andwait a few seconds for the
capacitor to discharge before removing the connections to the capacitor.

                                          GLOSSARY OF TERIS
                   (Explanation of terms as used in this Book.)

Bias - If the average mark is lengthened by the circuit, the circuit is said
       to have marking bias; if shortened, spacing bias. When referring to

       tubes, "bias" usually designates a grid or cathode potential.

Battery - This term is sometimes    used loosely to designate       any source  of di-
       rect current, particularly,  in this book, a rectifier       source.

Channel - In this book, "channel" designates the communication paot r eh quip-
       ment in the receiving circuit from a radio receiving antenna to the re-
       ceiving relay. With space diversityt,he relayis common to two channels.

Detector - A device for changing a-c signals to d-c signals.

Db - Abbreviation for decibels: Two amounts of power differ by N decibels
        according to the relation N = 10 logjg P,/Po. The number of decibels
        may be obtained from current ratios if the currents are measuirn eeqdual
       inpedances as follows: WN = 20 logjg I,/Ip-

Dbm - Abbreviation     for "db above or below      one milliwatt";  positive    sign in-
       dicates above,  negative sign below.

Frog - A term      derived from railroad designation     of a track crossing.     "To
        frog" two  circuits means to transpose them so  that each follows the   path
       which the   other followed previously.

Loop - A d-c extension line between a telegraph terminal and the printer and
       associated equipment.

Mark - A telegraph signaling interval durwhi ichncug rrent flows through the

printer magnet.        During this time, the circuit is said to be marking.

The interval during which no current flows through the printer magnet

is called a space.

Polar operation - Marking signals      are formed by    current pulses of one po-
        larity and spacing signals by  current pulses   of equal magnitude but of
       opposite polarity.

Rectifier - A device for changing alternating currentto direct current. In
        this book, it refers principally to the arrangements provided on the
       telegraph terminal bays for changing 50- to 60-cyclores25- to 60-cycle
       a-c power to 130-volts d-c poweirn ;the figures, the regular convention S e
        for a battery is used to indicate the rectifier.

Reversals - Repeated marks and spaces all of equal length.
Space - See Mark.

Space diversity - Refers to radio reception        in which two or more receivers
       are connected each to a separate antenna    and the outputs are combined.

              RADIO TELETYPE TERMINAL EQUIPMENT AN/FGCl or AN/FGC-1X  TM 11-356

Station --A printer and its associated equipment.

Telegraph     terminal  - This  term usually  designates  one bay of AN/FGCl  equip-
       ment.

Thermistor - A resistor whose resistance varies largely with temperature.

Varistor - A copper-oxide rectifier.
